Ibn 'Atiyya, Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di hold that their failure to know the truth stems from turning away from it rather than from its obscurity. Some readers recited "al-haqq" in the nominative, making the turning away itself the truth, a view noted by al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya, while the majority read it in the accusative. Al-Mawardi notes that the reminder may mean what is lawful and unlawful or pure monotheism, and presents both readings without deciding. The verse contains no legal ruling.

This verse states that no messenger sent before you was given any message other than this: there is no god but Me, so worship Me alone. The commentators read it as reinforcing the verses on divine unity that precede it. Al-Tabari, citing Qatada, reports that the messengers all came with sincerity and monotheism, while their laws differed in what was permitted and forbidden, in the Torah, the Gospel and the Qur'an alike. Ibn 'Atiyya adds that this creed never differed among the prophets, only the rulings did. Ibn Kathir explains that every book revealed to every prophet testifies that there is no god but God.

The immediate context is a rebuttal of those who claimed that the angels were God's daughters. Al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi understand the phrase about honoured servants as referring to the angels, who do not speak before God and act only on His command. Al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi attribute the claim to Khuza'a, the Quraysh, or the Jews, depending on the report. Al-Razi and Abu Hayyan develop the argument that multiple deities would lead to the corruption of the heavens and the earth.

On recitation, several scholars note that the reading with nun, followed by Hafs, Hamza and al-Kisa'i, expresses divine majesty, while the majority reading with ya is in the passive voice. Regarding intercession, Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid are cited with different interpretations, and the commentators do not settle between them.

This verse rejects the claim of some polytheists that the Most Merciful has taken a son. God glorifies Himself above such a claim and states that the angels are honoured servants. The commentators agree that servanthood is incompatible with being a son. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report that those who said this were the tribe of Khuza'a, who claimed the angels were God's daughters, and Ibn al-Jawzi also mentions Quraysh. Qatada adds that a similar claim was attributed to the Jews, who said God had married into the jinn. On the phrase 'they do not precede Him in speech', most explain that the angels speak and act only on His command, like well-mannered servants. Al-Zamakhshari reads 'honoured' as 'preferred over other servants', while Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Nasafi say the wording could include Jesus and Ezra if taken broadly. Commentators explain that the conditional threat of hell for an angel who claims divinity is a hypothetical meant to condemn association, and Qatada identifies this as Iblis. Finally, intercession is only for those whom God approves: Ibn 'Abbas takes this to mean the people of monotheism, and Mujahid to mean those God is pleased with, while all affirm that the angels are fearful of God.

This verse answers the claim of the polytheists that the Most Merciful has taken a child, since they said the angels are God's daughters. God declares Himself exalted above this and states that the angels are honoured servants, and that servanthood is incompatible with being a child. Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that "they do not precede Him in speech" means they speak only what their Lord commands and act only on His order, never opposing Him in word or deed. Sam'ani and Baghawi follow the same reading, while Ibn Juzayy sees it as a sign of courtesy toward God. Zamakhshari holds that the angels are preferred over all other servants, a view that Ibn al-Munayyir criticises as going beyond what the verse can bear. Several commentators, including Ibn Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi, record differing views on who is meant by the claim: the Quraysh or Khuza'a according to Ibn Abbas, the Jews or Christians according to Qatada. On intercession, Ibn Abbas and Mujahid agree that it applies only to those God approves of, whereas Hasan identifies them as those who profess the shahada. Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud note that the final conditional clause is hypothetical, and Qatada and Ibn Kathir take it to mean that God punishes any angel who would claim divinity.
The verse says that God knows what lies before and behind the angels, and that they intercede only for those whom He approves, while they stand in awe of Him.

This verse states that the angels, who are honoured servants, never speak before God and act only on His command, so none of them can claim divinity. Whoever among them would say, "I am a god besides Him," would be requited with Hell, and in the same way all wrongdoers who place divinity where it does not belong are requited. Most commentators understand the condition as hypothetical, since no angel actually said this.

Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, relying on Qatada and Ibn Juraij, report that the verse refers chiefly to Iblis, who called people to worship himself, and Qatada and al-Dahhak restrict it to him. Al-Tabari broadens the meaning to anyone who commits this kind of wrong. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi extend it to polytheists and to anyone who claims lordship, while al-Zamakhshari sees its main purpose as condemning association and magnifying the oneness of God.

There is broad agreement that the angels are servants rather than offspring, that servitude excludes filiation, and that they fear God with reverence. The commentators differ on the meaning of "those whom He approves": Ibn 'Abbas takes it to mean those who testify that there is no god but God, while Mujahid takes it to mean those whom God is pleased with. The Mu'tazilites use the phrase to deny intercession for grave sinners, whereas al-Razi and al-Qurtubi read it as evidence that intercession is granted to believers. Al-Razi, Ibn Sa'di and al-Shinqiti stress that this conditional form serves to reject association and does not assert that it will happen.

This verse rebukes those who disbelieve for not reflecting on the visible signs of creation: the heavens and the earth were once a joined mass that God separated, and He made water the origin of every living thing. The commentators broadly agree on this divine act of creation, but differ on the meaning of ratq and fatq. Ibn Abbas, Ata, Qatada, al-Hasan, al-Dahhak and Sa'id ibn Jubayr say the two were one stuck-together thing, which God parted with air, and Ka'b adds that a wind came between them. Mujahid, al-Suddi and Abu Salih hold that the heavens were a single layer that God split into seven heavens, and likewise the earth into seven earths. Ikrima, Ata and Ibn Zayd explain that the sky gave no rain and the earth produced no plants, so God opened the sky with rain and the earth with vegetation; al-Tabari and Ibn Atiyya prefer this reading, since the mention of water follows directly. Qatada and al-Hasan take the water to mean the origin of life, Qutrub and Abu al-Aliya take it to be the seminal fluid, while most understand the water that sustains life. Al-Razi reads the seeing as knowing rather than sight. The verse closes by censuring their refusal to believe.

The commentators explain that God set firm mountains on the earth so that it would not sway with its inhabitants, and made wide passages between them so that people could find their way to their destinations and livelihoods. Most agree that rawasi means mountains, that mayd means agitation or swaying, that fijaj means wide roads between two mountains, and that subul explains them. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report that the earth used to tip over with its people until God steadied it with mountains. Al-Tabari holds that the pronoun in fiha refers to the earth rather than the mountains, since the general meaning fits better, while Ibn 'Abbas, according to one transmission, takes it to mean the mountains, a view also followed by al-Razi and Ibn Kathir in one report. On the grammar of an tamid bihim, the Kufans hold that a negative la is understood, meaning so that it does not sway, whereas the Basrans and al-Zamakhshari read it as lest it sway out of dislike. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan note that placing fijaj before subul makes it a grammatical state and indicates that the roads were created wide. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur add that the guidance may be to the land's routes, or to reflection on God's oneness, and that some combine both meanings.

This verse states that God made the sky a roof for the earth, a well-protected one, yet the disbelievers turn away from its signs, namely the sun, the moon and the stars. The commentators agree on the apparent meaning: the sky is kept from falling onto the earth, as in the verse "He holds the heavens lest they fall upon the earth, except by His leave", cited by al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy. Al-Farra', al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi add that it is protected from devils by shooting stars, based on the verse "We guarded it from every accursed devil". Al-Razi holds that protection from falling is the stronger reading, since it is a greater blessing for mankind. Mujahid takes the word mahfuz to mean elevated. As for the signs, Mujahid, al-Tabari and al-Baghawi identify them as the sun, moon and stars, while Ibn Juzayy, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi include rain, thunder and lightning. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi describe turning away as failing to reflect on the precise order of their movements. The meaning of falak divides the scholars: Mujahid and al-Hasan compare it to a millstone, Ibn 'Abbas takes it to be the sky itself, Qatada sees an orbit in which the stars revolve, and others speak of a restrained wave. Al-Tabari declines to settle the question without conclusive evidence. All of them agree that the verb yasbahun means the swift motion of the heavenly bodies.

The commentators explain that this verse points to God's power and wisdom in creating night, day, the sun and the moon, each moving through an orbit in which it swims. Most agree that the pronoun in « yasbahun » refers to the sun and the moon along with similar bodies, and that the plural form used for rational beings describes them performing the act of swimming, as al-Farra' and Sibawayh note. Al-Zamakhshari adds that the tanwin on « kull » stands in for a dropped complement and that the sun and moon here stand for all their risings. On the meaning of « falak » opinions differ: Mujahid and al-Tabari compare it to a millstone, Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi take it to be the sky, Qatada describes a circular path in the sky where the stars turn, while most scholars hold it to be a moving wave beneath the sky in which the sun and moon travel, and al-Dahhak regards it as no body at all but the path of the stars. Ibn Kathir uses the image of a spindle turning in its whorl. Al-Tabari declines to choose one view for lack of a sound text, while al-Razi and al-Baydawi list the positions and lean toward the orbit being fixed with the stars swimming within it. Al-Sha'rawi connects the verb to the movement of a fish in water.

God tells His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ that He did not grant immortality to any human before him, and that death awaits every soul. If he dies, those who were waiting for his death will not be immortal either; the verse answers those who said they would wait for the vicissitudes of time to take him. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi agree that death is an unavoidable path for every living being and that the verse does not permit gloating over a dead person. Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Sa'di draw from it that al-Khidr has died because he is a human being, while al-Tha'alibi and al-Alusi consider this inference not conclusive. As for the particle fa-in and the interrogative form, al-Farra' explains that it marks the condition and carries the sense of denial, whereas Sibawayh and Yunus differ on where the question falls, without any legal consequence. On the phrase every soul shall taste death, the commentators describe it as the bitterness of the soul leaving the body. God tests people with evil and good, meaning hardship and ease, illness and health, wealth and poverty, to see who gives thanks and who is patient, and then they will be returned to Him for recompense. Ibn Zayd and al-Qurtubi explain that good and evil here mean what people love and what they dislike, while Ibn 'Atiyya holds that they mean what can serve as a trial, such as wealth and bodily health, excluding guidance and misguidance.

The verse states that every soul will taste death, and that God tests people in this world with evil and good, meaning hardship and ease, poverty and wealth, sickness and health, before they return to Him for reckoning and recompense. The commentators agree that the test reveals whether a person bears hardship with patience and gives thanks for good, and that God treats people as one who tests them, although He knows their deeds before they occur. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi report, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, that good and evil mean adversity and prosperity, illness and health, wealth and poverty. Ibn Zayd understands them as what people love and what they dislike. Al-Mawardi offers a wider reading: evil may be the dominance of desire over the soul and good may be protection from sin, a view he attributes to al-Tustari and Sahl ibn 'Abd Allah. Ibn 'Atiyya argues that guidance and misguidance, and obedience and disobedience, are not part of this test, since guidance is not itself a trial, while other commentators keep the verse general. On the occasion of revelation, some say the pagans were waiting for the Prophet's death, while others say some Muslims believed he would never die. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi explain that tasting death means perceiving its pains and beginnings, and that the generality of the verse is restricted. Al-Alusi holds that the soul meant is the animal soul and notes the disagreement about whether angels die. Ibn 'Ashur presents life as a period of trial in which good and evil mingle, and this world as a house of testing.

This verse describes how the disbelievers treat the Prophet ﷺ when they see him: they take him only as an object of mockery, saying to one another, "Is this the one who speaks ill of your gods?" Most commentators note that dhikr can mean praise or blame, and that the context here points to blame, that is, disparaging the idols. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that the disbelievers did not recognise the name al-Rahman and knew only Musaylima. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Ibn Atiyya take the reference to be the revelation or the affirmation of God's oneness, while Ibn Ashur and al-Alusi see their rejection as directed at the Qur'an. The following clause points to the paradox: they object to their powerless gods being mentioned while they themselves disbelieve in the Merciful. On the phrase "man was created of haste", opinions differ. Some apply it to Adam, whose haste is recounted by Mujahid and Ibn Kathir, others to humankind in general, and Qatada sees it as a natural disposition. Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan consider the figurative reading the most sound. Some also explain ajal as "clay", citing a Himyarite line, although Ibn Atiyya finds this unconvincing. The commentators agree that the verse warns those who hasten the punishment that God's signs will come, notably at Badr according to al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir.

The commentators explain that the words "Man was created of haste" mean that hastiness is rooted in human nature, which rushes toward what it loves and toward what it fears. The verse addresses the idolaters who demanded punishment: God promises to show them His signs and forbids them to hasten it. Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Suddi, al-Kalbi and Muqatil take "man" here to mean Adam: when the spirit reached his head and eyes he tried to stand before his creation was complete, or he was created at the end of Friday and was hurried so that he would be finished before sunset. Qatada, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi favour the reading that man was made prone to haste. Ibn 'Abbas, in one report, and al-Nadr ibn al-Harith are named as the intended individual, as he demanded punishment. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi argue that the prohibition does not impose the impossible, since God gave man the power to restrain his haste. Abu 'Ubayda and several lexicographers explain "ajal" as clay in the Himyarite dialect, while others read an inversion in which haste was drawn out of man. Readers differ over "khuliqa" and "khalaqa", the majority reading being the former. As for the "signs", some understand them as worldly punishments such as the battle of Badr, others as the proofs of God's oneness and the Prophet's truthfulness. The blamed haste is the question "When will this promise come?"

This verse reports that the disbelievers asked, with mockery and challenge, when the promise that the Prophet and the believers warned them of would come, and doubted that they were truthful. The commentators explain that the question expresses impatience and derision rather than a real request to fix a date. On what the 'promise' refers to, opinions differ: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi understand it as the punishment the Prophet threatened, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya also mention punishment in the Hereafter or the Last Hour, and Ibn Juzayy and al-Nasafi take it as the Resurrection or the arrival of punishment. Ibn 'Ashur adds that the question was also aimed at the Muslims, who were asking for the promised victory, and that it was used ironically, since the polytheists were certain the promise would not come true. Most commentators take the address in 'if you are truthful' to be to the Prophet and the believers. Al-Tabari and al-Jalalayn treat 'matā' as an accusative of time, whereas Ibn 'Atiyya, Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi place it in the nominative, which they regard as the sounder view. The commentators agree that the verse answers these mockers by affirming that the threat is certain, that haste is part of human nature, and that the answer to their question is implied.

This verse describes the condition of the disbelievers on the Day of Judgment. The commentators explain that if they knew the moment they demanded by asking "When is this promise?", when the fire will surround them from every side so that they cannot ward it off from their faces or their backs, and no one will help them, they would not hurry and would not persist in disbelief. There is general agreement that the answer to "law" is omitted and implied by the context, and that this omission makes the threat more forceful. They also agree that the faces and backs are mentioned because they are the most honoured and most exposed parts of the body, so that surrounding them means surrounding the whole body. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi describe the fire striking the faces and burning the backs, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi stress total encirclement. Al-Baghawi reports the view that the backs are struck with whips. The verses that follow state that the Hour will come suddenly, overwhelm them and leave them bewildered, with no power to repel it and no respite for repentance. Al-Tabari adds that this is a time of recompense, not of action. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi link the passage to consoling the Prophet, since earlier messengers were also mocked and their mockers were punished. On the word 'ajal in the next verse, most scholars take the human being to be Adam, while others take it to mean humankind in general or al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, and some propose an inversion of the sentence, a view that al-Razi and al-Nahhas reject.

This verse says that the punishment of the disbelievers will come suddenly, when they do not expect it. It will bewilder them so that they cannot push it away, and they will be given no respite. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi understand it as referring to the Hour or the Day of Resurrection, a time of recompense rather than of action, in which no delay for repentance is possible. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan take the pronoun in tatihim to refer to the Fire, while al-Zamakhshari also allows that it may refer to the promise or to the time, and al-Baydawi mentions the same range of options. For the verb tabhatuhum, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain it as leaving them bewildered, whereas Ibn Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi render it as taking them by surprise and overpowering them. On the phrase they will not be given respite, al-Baghawi and Ibn Atiyya gloss it as they will not be delayed, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Ashur see it as a reminder of the long respite God had granted them earlier. Al-A'mash read the verbs with a initial ya, which makes the pronoun refer to the promise. Ibn Ashur links the verse to the events of Badr, while most commentators apply it to the afterlife.

In this verse God consoles His Prophet ﷺ by reminding him that messengers before him were also mocked by their peoples, and that the punishment they were ridiculed for mentioning eventually befell those who scoffed. The commentators broadly agree on this plain meaning. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the verb haqqa means to befall or surround, and that what was mocked was the punishment the prophets warned of. Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi also stress that the verse gives the Prophet a promise: what his opponents do to him will fall back on them, as it did on the mockers of earlier prophets.

The context is the taunts of the Quraysh, who, according to Abu Hayyan and al-Shawkani, asked whether this was the one who speaks ill of their gods. The verse belongs to a passage about the unbelievers' eagerness to demand punishment, and the commentators read it in that light.

Opinions differ on the exact sense of the word ma in "what they used to mock". Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi take it to be the punishment itself. Az-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi understand it as the requital for their mockery, and Abu al-Su'ud adds that it could even be their mockery itself, appearing in the hereafter in a substantial form. Ibn 'Atiyya notes that the word "requital" must be understood, and observes that the verse combines consolation for the Prophet with a warning to the disbelievers.

God instructs His Prophet to ask those who mock and demand punishment: who will guard you by night and by day from the Most Merciful? For most commentators the question is one of rebuke and denial: no one can shield you from Him. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi explain the verb yaklaʾukum as protecting and guarding, and Ibn Kathir reads min as meaning instead of, while others take it as from His punishment. The verse then states that the cause of their heedlessness is their turning away from the remembrance of their Lord, that is the Quran and its admonitions. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi conclude that they do not even bring God to mind, let alone fear His might, and will only recognise the protector once they are afflicted; Abu al-Su'ud restricts the turning away to the reminder suited to their condition. Al-Tabari sees bal as confirming a denial that the listeners already know. The commentators agree that their idols can neither defend themselves nor be accompanied by divine support, but they differ on yusḥabūn: protected according to Ibn Abbas and al-Tabari, prevented according to others, helped according to Mujahid. Ibn al-Qayyim notes that God guards His servants day and night despite being wholly independent of them. Ibn 'Ashur and al-Shinqiti retain an interrogative sense that works as both denial and statement, and hold that true protection belongs to God alone.

This verse denies that the polytheists have any deities able to shield them from God's punishment. The commentators explain its meaning as follows: do those who hasten the punishment have gods that would protect them if God sent His scourge upon them? The verse then describes these gods as powerless, since one who cannot defend himself cannot defend others. The scholars differ on the phrase 'nor are they accompanied by Us'. Ibn Abbas, Ata and al-Tabari take it to mean that they are not granted protection or shelter against punishment, relying on the Arabic idiom 'I am your protector against so-and-so'. Mujahid, and another report from Ibn Abbas, understand it as having no one to support or defend them, while Qatada reads it as meaning that God does not accompany them with any good. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi note that the gods cannot defend themselves and receive no divine help, so they cannot help others. According to Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi, the pronoun 'they' refers to the disbelievers according to Ibn Abbas, and to the idols according to Qatada. For al-Sa'di and al-Qasimi, what follows explains why they are deceived: God granted them provision and long life, while the land is diminished from its edges, a sign of their decline, which al-Tabari and al-Baydawi interpret as the spread of Islam.

The commentators explain that this verse answers the idolaters who grew proud because they enjoyed blessings and long life, assuming that their gods protected them. In truth God alone is the Guardian, and they took no lesson from the fate of those before them. As for the phrase « We come upon the land, reducing it from its edges », opinions differ. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Hasan take it to mean the spread of Islam and the conquest of lands of unbelief, one land after another, a view that Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn 'Ashur also favour from the context. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Abi Talha understand it as the ruin of towns and the loss of their blessing, while Ata' and al-Dahhak speak of the death of scholars and jurists, and al-Kalbi of killing and captivity. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi limit it to describing Muslim campaigns into the lands of the idolaters. Ibn Kathir links the passage to the ruined towns mentioned in Surat al-Ahqaf, and al-Shinqiti sees in it a warning to the Quraysh. All agree that the question « Are they then the victors? » is a rebuke, victory belonging to God, His messenger and the believers. Al-Razi notes that the surah is Meccan, so the reduction must be understood as fewer unbelievers through people entering Islam, a view Ibn 'Ashur adopts. The commentators also discuss the meaning of « yakla'uka » (to guard) and of « yuṣḥabūna », which is read as being protected, helped or granted good.

This verse tells the Prophet to say that he warns people only through the Revelation, meaning the Quran sent down by God, and not through anything of his own. Qatada identifies the Revelation with this Quran, and al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Kathir give the same sense. The phrase that the deaf do not hear the call is read by most commentators as a picture of the disbelievers: they are deaf to the Book of God, gain nothing from what they hear and do not understand it, like a deaf person who does not hear what is said to him. This is the view of al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi, al-Baydawi and the Jalalayn. Al-Zamakhshari notes that the definite article in the deaf points back to those being warned, and that the noun is used instead of a pronoun to show their deliberate deafness to warning.

The readings differ. Most readers have yā' with fatha, so that the verb is active with God or the subject understood, whereas Ibn ‘Amir reads a feminine form with the Prophet as the addressee and the deaf in the accusative; Ibn ‘Atiyya considers this reading weak. Al-Tabari also reports that Abu ‘Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami read it in the passive, which would mean God does not make the deaf hear.

The following verse is usually read together with this one. According to the commentators, if even a slight breath of the punishment of your Lord touched them, they would cry out, 'Woe to us, we were wrongdoers.' Ibn ‘Abbas takes 'nafha' as a small portion, Qatada as punishment, and Ibn Jurayj as a share, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi stress the force of the image of a passing whiff.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the idolaters who were hastening the punishment: if even the slightest touch of it reached them, they would admit their wrongdoing and cry out for their own destruction. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take nafha to mean a portion or a punishment, while Ibn Abbas and Ibn Kaysan understand it as a small amount or a slight touch, and Ibn Jurayj links it to the phrase 'he gave him a share of his wealth', meaning a modest portion. They agree that the wrongdoing they confess is associating partners with God and rejecting the Messenger, and that this confession will come too late to help them. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari point out several emphatic features: the verb 'touch', the sense of smallness inherent in nafha, the singular form that denotes a single occurrence, and the indefinite noun. Abu Hayyan and Ibn Ashur repeat these observations. As to when this touch occurs, al-Alusi notes that it may be on the Day of Resurrection, whereas others, following Ibn Abbas, identify it with the hunger that struck Mecca. The verses that follow in the text continue with the setting up of the just scales on the Day of Judgement, when no soul will be wronged even by the weight of a mustard seed.

This verse says that God will set up scales of justice on the Day of Resurrection, so that no soul will be wronged in the least, and even the weight of a mustard seed will be brought and reckoned. God is sufficient as a reckoner. The commentators agree on the absolute justice of the scales and that God does not wrong anyone. They differ on whether the scale is real. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Juzayy, following the majority of the People of the Sunna, take it to be a real balance with two pans and a beam, in which deeds or their records are weighed. Al-Hasan described it the same way. Mujahid, Qatada and al-Dahhak, and according to al-Tabari a report from Ibn Abbas, read it as a figure for justice in recompense, a view Ibn Ashur inclines towards. Al-Razi and al-Alusi hold the scale to be literal and note that the Mu'tazila denied it. On the plural 'mawazin', most say it is one scale, the plural reflecting the many deeds weighed, while Ibn Ashur does not rule out several scales. The word 'qist' is generally taken as a verbal noun used for emphasis, or as an elision of 'possessors of justice'. Readers differ over the case of 'mithqal', but the meaning remains much the same.

This verse states that God gave Moses and Aaron the Furqan, the Book that separates truth from falsehood, as well as a light that illuminates the darkness of ignorance and a reminder for the God-fearing. Most commentators understand the Furqan here to mean the Torah, which distinguishes the lawful from the unlawful and sets out the laws. Mujahid, Qatada and Abu Salih take this view, and al-Tabari reports that some hold it as well.

Other meanings have been proposed for the Furqan. Ibn Zayd took it to be the proof that separated Moses' truth from Pharaoh's falsehood, or victory over enemies, as in the Day of the Furqan. Ibn Abbas understood it as the decisive victory, al-Dahhak as the parting of the sea, and Muhammad ibn Ka'b as the deliverance from doubts. Al-Tabari preferred Ibn Zayd's view because of the conjunction before 'light', while al-Zajjaj held that such a conjunction is not dropped and that 'light' describes the Torah as an additional attribute.

Regarding 'those who fear their Lord in secret', most say they fear God without having seen Him. Muqatil relates it to fear of His punishment, and al-Zajjaj to fear of God when no one sees them. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Atiyya lean towards fear in private. Being 'apprehensive of the Hour' means being seized with dread of the terrors of the Last Day.

Many commentators, including Ibn Kathir and al-Razi, connect the passage to a consolation for the Prophet, recalling what earlier messengers received. The address then turns to the Quran as a blessed reminder whose rejection is presented as baffling.

This passage recalls that God gave Moses and Aaron the Criterion, which most commentators take to be the Torah, since it distinguishes truth from falsehood. It is also a light and a reminder for the God-fearing. The verse then describes these pious people as those who fear their Lord in the unseen, that is, in private when no one watches, and who are anxious about the terrors of the Hour. Al-Tabari, al-Mawardi and al-Nasafi take this description as praise of the pious, while Ibn Kathir reads it as stressing their fear of God even when they cannot see Him. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi note that the relative clause may be a qualifier or a separate praise. On the meaning of unseen, Ibn Abbas and Mujahid understand it as fear of a punishment not yet visible, al-Zajjaj as fear of a God who cannot see them, and al-Razi holds that the fear is inward and shows itself most in private. Ibn al-Qayyim describes ishfaq as a fear joined with tenderness. The verse connects to what follows: the Quran is a blessed reminder that should not be denied, just as the Torah was given before it.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the Qur'an as a reminder (dhikr) through which whoever remembers is admonished, and as a blessed revelation abundant in good. God sent it down to Muhammad ﷺ, and then rebukes the disbelievers with a question of reproach about their denial of a book whose nature is plain. The verse belongs to a passage about the Torah given to Moses and Aaron, the Qur'an being presented as comparable to it in its descent and guidance. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and others read the 'reminder' as admonition, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Ibn 'Ashur understand 'blessed' as abundant benefit. Ibn 'Ashur sees in the demonstrative the Qur'an's presence in minds and recitation, and al-Biqa'i holds that denial is all the more blameworthy from Arabs who know the worth of Moses' Book. There is broad agreement that the question is a rebuke and that it consoles the Prophet. The commentators differ more on the 'criterion' (furqan) mentioned just before: al-Tabari, Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Kathir take it to be the Torah that separates truth from falsehood, while Ibn Zayd takes it to be victory over enemies, a view al-Tha'alibi and al-Qurtubi support by pointing to the day of Badr. They also discuss the meaning of 'light' and 'reminder', and a reading attributed to Ibn 'Abbas without the conjunction, some judging the waw to be superfluous, a view rejected by al-Zajjaj. Finally, fearing God 'in the unseen' is read by the commentators as fearing a God not seen, fearing His punishment, or fearing Him in private, and dread of the Hour means fear of its terrors. The commentators set out these views without deciding between them.

This verse states that God granted Abraham his rushd, meaning his right guidance, before the time of Moses and Aaron, and that God knew he was worthy of it. The commentators differ on what rushd means. Al-Tabari, Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Kathir understand it as divine guidance from childhood, shown in his rejection of his father's and people's idolatry, and Ibn al-Jawzi reports that this happened before puberty. Al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi take it to mean prophethood, or as a broader rectitude that includes prophethood. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and al-Razi explain that God's knowledge of him means that He had seen in him admirable qualities and pleasing traits that made him fit to be His intimate friend. As for "before", al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir take it to mean before Moses and Aaron, while Ibn al-Qayyim holds that the soundest view is before the revelation of the Torah, and Ibn Ashur sees it as a reference to the sequence of prophets. Some, such as al-Sam'ani and Ibn al-Jawzi, also mention the period before his mission or even before his birth. All these readings agree on an early divine choice and preparation of Abraham, which introduces the story of his confrontation with idolatry.

This verse recalls Ibrahim's question to his father and people about the images to which they remained devoted. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi, identify these images as idols, and explain that the question was asked in a mocking, belittling tone although Ibrahim knew well what they were. They agree that this passage belongs to the story of Ibrahim with his people, and that the guidance mentioned in the previous verse, his rushd, refers to the right direction Allah granted him. They differ on the phrase min qabl: some, such as al-Razi, take it as before his maturity, others as before Moses and Aaron. Ibn al-Qayyim considers the most correct view to be before the revelation of the Torah. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi explain that the verb for remaining devoted implies constant worship, and that the particle la indicates ownership or purpose rather than transitivity. The people replied that they had found their fathers worshipping them, and Ibrahim answered that they and their fathers were in clear error. Commentators see in this reply a rebuke of blind imitation without proof.

The verse reports the answer of Abraham's people when he rebuked them for worshipping idols: they said they had found their fathers worshipping them and had followed them. The commentators read this as an admission of blind imitation with no proof. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Mahalli and al-Suyuti explain that they followed their ancestors in this worship, and Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Qurtubi, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi say much the same. All agree that Abraham's reply, that they and their fathers were in clear error, shows that a falsehood does not become true because many hold it; al-Razi, Abu Hayyan and Abu al-Sud develop this point. On grammar, al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan note that the verb 'akafa' takes the preposition lam here, giving the sense of constant devotion, whereas Abu al-Sud prefers to understand an implied sense of worship. Ibn Kathir adds that the Israelite reports about Abraham's youth may be accepted only where they agree with authentic texts. For Ibn Sa'di and Sayyid Qutb the verse condemns blind imitation, which paralyses thought, while faith calls for examining every matter and weighing its true value.

This verse recounts Abraham's reply to his father and people, who had challenged him for refusing to join their worship. He tells them that they and their fathers were in clear error, which no sensible person could miss, because their worship rested on blind imitation rather than on any proof. Most commentators understand the address to include both the imitators and those they followed. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain the error as straying from the path of truth and deviating from the straight way, while al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi note that the emphatic "you yourselves" is needed to permit coordination with the pronoun, and that the preposition "in" signals a settled, firmly rooted error. Al-Tabari and al-Baghawi take "manifest" to mean plain to anyone who reflects with his intellect. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi offer several readings of the word "rushd": prophethood, rightness of judgment, or guidance toward what is good, and al-Qurtubi reports that most exegetes take it as the guidance Abraham received before his prophethood. Al-Razi also uses the verse in a theological debate about whether faith is created by God. The commentators agree that the reply denounces unquestioning imitation of ancestors, and al-Sha'rawi adds that faith cannot be built on tradition alone. Al-Muyassar keeps to the general sense of distance from the truth without entering into these debates.

This verse reports the reaction of Abraham's people when he rejected the worship of idols. They asked, in astonishment, whether he was speaking in earnest or was merely joking. According to al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir, they did not believe that what he said was serious; they set truth, meaning seriousness, against play and jest, and the question expressed surprise and rejection more than a genuine search for information.

The commentators agree that this question answers Abraham's claim that they and their fathers were in clear error, and that they had only the imitation of their ancestors to offer as justification. Al-Razi explains that they could not imagine he would oppose them with such seriousness. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi note that the nominal sentence used for the option of play shows they considered it more likely. Ibn 'Ashur and al-Alusi describe the question as rhetorical, and al-Alusi treats the particle 'am' as disjunctive rather than connective, relying on a reading he attributes to al-Tibi. The commentators do not settle between these readings.

Abraham's answer that follows shifts the discussion to the declaration that the Lord of the heavens and the earth, who created them, is the one true Lord, which most exegetes present as evidence of the seriousness of his call.

This verse reports that when his people asked whether he was serious or joking, Abraham set aside the jest and declared that their Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth, the One who created them, and that he bears witness to this. Commentators differ on what «fatarahunna» refers to: al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy take it as referring to the heavens and the earth, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi, followed by Abu al-Su'ud, prefer that it refers to the idols, since this deepens their error and strengthens the argument against them; Ibn 'Atiyya sees it as a way of speaking of the idols as if they understood. On «min al-shahidin», al-Tabari, al-Sam'ani and Ibn Kathir read it as a testimony that God alone is the deity deserving worship, whereas al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi read it as a demonstration by proof, and al-Biqa'i adds that a witness is one able to establish the evidence. The commentators go on to report that Abraham then vowed to plot against their idols, breaking them in pieces while they were away and leaving the largest one so that they would turn back to it, as al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Juzayy explain; Ibn Kathir and al-Tha'alibi relate narratives about this episode that they treat with caution. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the question «what are these statues» is posed in feigned ignorance. All agree that the verse rejects blind imitation of ancestors and that Abraham's words were meant in earnest.

In this verse Abraham tells his people, as the commentators explain it, that he will devise a plot against their idols once they have turned away and gone off to their festival. Most commentators take the word kayd to mean a scheme or stratagem aimed at breaking the idols, while al-Sam'ani notes that it can also resemble open combat. Ibn 'Ashur observes that Abraham, having already opposed idolatry with argument, now declares his intention to change the wrong with his hand.

The commentators agree that Abraham spoke these words in private, and that only one man, or a group of weaker people who had stayed behind, heard them. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report that the people set out for their festival and that Abraham pretended to be ill so he could remain. Al-Zamakhshari reports that there were seventy idols and that Abraham left only the largest one intact. Ibn al-Jawzi gives the number as seventy-two.

Opinions differ on why the verb for scheming is used of idols that cannot act. Al-Razi explains it as a figurative usage, since the people believed the idols could be harmed; others read it as meaning that Abraham would trap the people through their idols. Al-Sa'di holds that Abraham wanted to show the idols' helplessness in practice, and al-Sha'rawi sees the breaking of the idols as a practical proof of the error of worshipping them. Al-Baydawi notes that the letter ta in "tallahi" expresses wonder at how difficult the task is.

The commentators explain that after the people had gone out to their festival and Abraham stayed behind claiming sickness, he smashed their idols into pieces, sparing only the largest and hanging the axe around its neck, so that the people would return to him, the idols' helplessness would be exposed and the proof would be established against them. Most, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi, agree that judhadhan means fragments or shattered pieces, and that the different readings are close in meaning, al-Tabari preferring the damma reading because the readers agree on it. They differ on what 'ilayhi' refers to: al-Razi, Abu Hayyan and al-Baydawi, followed by most, take it to be Abraham, who would then confront and silence them, whereas al-Kalbi, as reported by Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi, takes it to be the largest idol, whom they would ask about the breaking, and some take it to be God. Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Nasafi record further explanations for sparing the largest idol. Zamakhshari suggests Abraham acted on his judgement of their stubbornness or even mockingly, knowing they would not return to him. Commentators present Abraham's words as an argumentative challenge rather than a lie, and Ibn Kathir cites the hadith of the three statements in this connection. Al-Sa'di adds that the believer should avoid honouring what God has belittled unless it is attributed to those who honour it.

The verse describes the reaction of Abraham's people when they returned from their festival and found their idols smashed: they asked, in outrage, who had done this to their gods, declaring that the perpetrator was a wrongdoer. The commentators explain this wrongdoing in several ways: as audacity towards gods deserving veneration, as excessive destruction and contempt, or as exposing oneself to ruin. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi share the general sense of wrongdoing as transgression, while Ibn Ashur notes that the act refers to the destruction of the idols. Some, such as Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Atiyya, take the interrogative as a question of inquiry and reproach, whereas al-Zamakhshari reads it as a plain statement of guilt. The following verses show that they then recalled a young man who had threatened the idols. The exegetes agree that 'before the eyes of the people' means publicly. They differ on the purpose: al-Tabari, al-Hasan and Qatada say the aim was to have witnesses to the act, while Ibn Ishaq says they wanted the people to witness the punishment. Al-Qurtubi draws the lesson that no one should be punished on a mere claim without evidence.

The commentators explain that when Abraham's people returned from their festival and found their idols smashed, they asked who had done it. Some of those who had heard Abraham swear that he would plot against their idols answered that they had heard a young man called Abraham disparaging them. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi agree that "yadhkuruhum" means that he blames, reviles and belittles them, and that "Ibrahim" is the name by which this youth is called. On the word "fata", al-Tabari, al-Nasafi and al-Qurtubi take it to mean a young man, and al-Qurtubi relates Ibn Abbas's saying that God sent no prophet except as a young man.

The commentators also agree that "in the sight of the people" means openly, before everyone, in public. On "so that they may bear witness", opinions differ. Al-Hasan, Qatada and al-Suddi understand it as testimony against him for what he did, since they did not want to seize him without proof. Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Kathir understand it as witnessing his punishment. Ibn al-Jawzi reports a third view, that they would testify to his words against their gods. Al-Qurtubi draws from this that no one should be prosecuted on a mere accusation without evidence.

Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Ibn Atiyya discuss the grammatical role of "Ibrahim". The most widely held view, adopted by al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and al-Nasafi, is that it is the subject of a passive verb, the intended meaning being the name itself rather than the person.

This verse reports the words of Abraham's people after they returned from their festival and found their idols smashed. They asked who had done this, and some of them said they had heard a young man called Abraham disparaging the idols, so they ordered that he be brought "before the eyes of the people", meaning openly and in full view. The commentators differ on the meaning of "that they may bear witness". Al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi, citing al-Hasan, Qatada and al-Suddi, say it means that people would testify against him for what he had done, since they disliked punishing him without proof. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak and Ibn Ishaq hold that it means they wanted people to witness his punishment, a reading Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur favour. Al-Mawardi also mentions testimony to what he said. Al-Tabari argues that mere presence would have been phrased differently, which points towards testimony. Al-Alusi and Abu al-Su'ud note that the wording also carries a sense of hope, and that the phrase can refer either to the punishment or to the testimony. The commentators agree that the matter was thus made public, which gave Abraham the opportunity to bring the truth before the assembly.

After Abraham was brought before the people, they asked him whether he had done this to their gods. He answered that their chief idol had done it, and invited them to ask the idols if they could speak. The commentators agree that this answer served as proof against them and a rebuke, showing that the idols cannot speak or defend themselves. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report that the people brought him publicly so that they could witness his punishment, and that Abraham wanted the truth to be made clear before everyone. On how his reply should be understood, opinions differ: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi see it as an argument aimed at establishing the proof against them; al-Farra, al-Kisa'i, Ibn Qutayba and al-Zamakhshari place it among indirect speech (ma'arid) that avoids a plain lie; al-Razi and Ibn al-Arabi see it as a way of showing that one who has no power cannot be a god. Most cite the hadith narrated by Abu Hurayra about Abraham's three lies, and some consider that it was not a true lie. When they briefly reflected and admitted their error, the commentators say, they relapsed into obstinacy and claimed that Abraham knew the idols could not speak.

This verse records Abraham's reply when his people asked whether he had broken their idols: he said that the largest of them had done it, and told them to ask the idols if they can speak. The commentators agree that this was a rebuke and a proof against them, since whatever cannot speak or defend itself does not deserve worship. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir say the aim was to establish the argument and show them their error, relying on the authentic hadith that Abraham told only three lies, among them this statement; al-Tabari holds that God may have permitted this for a good purpose, as He permitted the crier of Joseph. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Alusi read it as an indirect speech (ma'arid) that reaches its goal without outright falsehood, and Ibn al-Jawzi notes that many scholars took this line. Ibn Juzayy, by contrast, accepts that the statement is outwardly false though not meant as a real claim. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur stress that the statement was meant to make them reflect on the nature of their idols. Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' offered different readings and grammatical analyses, which Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi discuss. Ibn Kathir reports that after they came to themselves and admitted their wrong, they turned back to stubbornness, and Sayyid Qutb sees the words as a serious mockery rather than a lie.

This verse describes the moment when Abraham's people came back to their senses after the largest idol showed them its helplessness. The commentators say they returned to their reason and reflected, and then admitted that the wrongdoers were themselves, not Abraham. They differ on what this wrong consisted of: Ibn 'Abbas took it to be worshipping what cannot speak, Wahb ibn Munabbih to have abandoned their gods unguarded or worshipped the small ones alongside the great one, while Ibn Ishaq and Muqatil took it to be their accusation against Abraham while the axe was still on the great idol's neck. Al-Tabari also reports that some understood it as a speaking of some to others. On the phrase 'then they were turned upside down on their heads', al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur explain it as a relapse into argument after almost accepting the truth, Ibn Qutayba as a return to their earlier view that the idols do not speak, and Ibn al-Jawzi also cites confusion (Qatada). Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Ibn Juzayy read it as a figure for their fall back into error, and Ibn Juzayy also allows that they literally lowered their heads in shame. The commentators agree that the proof, though clear, met with stubbornness.

This verse describes what happened after Abraham's people came to their senses and admitted their own wrongdoing when he was questioned about the smashed idols. The commentators explain the phrase "then they were turned back upon their heads" as a return to error after that admission: they told Abraham that he knew these idols cannot speak, so how could he ask them to answer? Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir note that the root naks means to turn something over so that its top becomes its bottom, and that the expression here is a metaphor for reverting from the truth.

Most exegetes, including Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Kathir, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Nasafi, take it that the people returned to idolatry after confessing the truth. Az-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi offer other readings: they bowed their heads in shame or confusion, or they were simply defeated in argument. Al-Alusi considers the last reading the most apparent. As-Suddi held that they fell back into strife, Ibn Zayd that they went astray in opinion, and Qatada that a disastrous bewilderment seized them.

The commentators also differ on the reading "nukkisu" with doubled letter, which az-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and Ibn al-Jawzi report as a minority reading in which the people themselves are the subject of the turning over. Abu al-Su'ud notes that the text does not say they lowered their heads, which weakens the reading of shame. After this retort, Abraham rebuked them by asking why they worship what neither benefits nor harms them.

This verse records Abraham's response to his people after they had been forced to admit that their idols cannot speak. He asks them how they can worship, besides God, things that bring them no benefit if they worship them and no harm if they abandon them. He then expresses disgust at them and their deities and urges them to use their reason. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi, agree that the verse denies divinity to idols, which are powerless to help or harm. The word 'uff' is explained as an expression of disgust, foulness or annoyance. Scholars differ on the phrase 'they were turned back upon their heads': Qatada and Ibn Qutayba take it to mean that they returned to their former error, al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi read it as a metaphor for confused reasoning, and al-Tabari sees it as the collapse of their own argument. Several add that, having lost the debate, they turned to violence and proposed burning him. Al-Razi, al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan discuss Abraham's remark that 'their largest one did it'. Most read it as a rhetorical argument rather than a lie, though al-Razi reports the view of those who considered it a genuine falsehood and defends it by context. Some commentaries, such as Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, go on to relate accounts of the fire, many of which their own authors judge weak. Al-Jalalayn, al-Sa'di and al-Jaza'iri keep to the plain sense: useless idols do not deserve worship.

The commentators explain that this verse belongs to Abraham's argument with his people. He expresses his disgust at their worship of idols that neither benefit nor harm them and cannot speak: "Uff to you and to what you worship besides Allah! Will you not then use your reason?" They agree that "uff" is a cry of distaste and impatience, and that the lam indicates who is the object of this disgust, namely the people and their gods. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir place the verse after the proof has been made: the people admitted that their idols do not speak, then returned to their stubbornness and proposed burning him. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur read the phrase "turned upon their heads" as an image of their relapse into error after nearly admitting the truth, whereas Qatada and Ibn al-Jawzi understand it as their bewilderment. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Baydawi explain that Abraham's irritation came from seeing his people persist in idolatry once the truth had become clear, and that the rebuke concerns their failure to use their intellect. All agree that the closing question is a reproach and a denial. Disagreement mainly concerns the context of the passage and the meaning of "turned upon their heads", not the sense of the verse itself.

This verse describes how Abraham's people, having been unable to answer his arguments against idol worship, turned to force. Some of them told the others to burn him and to avenge their gods, if they were truly going to help them. The commentators agree that fire was considered the most dreadful punishment, and that this response came from anger at their defeat in argument. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi all report that God commanded the fire to become cool and safe for Abraham, so that it burned nothing of him except his bonds, and that when he was thrown in he said: God is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs. The identity of the one who proposed the burning is disputed. Ibn Umar, Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj say he was a Kurdish man from the Persian desert dwellers, while al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Ashur name Nimrod, and a report cited by al-Baghawi and al-Zamakhshari says the earth swallowed him up. The detailed accounts of gathering the wood, the catapult and the length of his stay in the fire vary widely, and several scholars, including Ibn Kathir, Ibn Juzayy and al-Sa'di, regard many of them as unreliable or do not dwell on them. Modern commentators such as al-Sha'rawi and al-Jaza'iri stress that the scheme turned against its planners, who were the real losers, while Abraham's safety was a sign from God.

In plain terms, the commentators explain that God commanded the fire to become cool and safe for Ibrahim (peace be upon him), so that it did no harm to him even though his people had thrown him into it to defend their idols. It was a miracle that broke the usual order of nature. Al-Tabari, al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi agree that the fire burned only his bonds, and that the word "salaman" protects him from an excessive cold that could have killed him had the verse said only "coolness", as reported from Ibn Abbas, Ali and Abu al-Aliya. Opinions differ on how the fire became cool. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi say God removed from the fire its nature of burning while keeping its light; others say God repelled its harm from Ibrahim's body, or placed a barrier between them; al-Razi and most scholars prefer the first view as closest to the apparent meaning. As for who spoke the command, al-Sudi says it was Gabriel, while most say it was God Himself. Many commentators narrate lengthy accounts of the story, but Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and Ibn Juzayy hold that only what the Qur'an states is sound, and that much of the rest belongs to Israelite narratives. All agree that the plot of Ibrahim's people was the burning, and that God made them the greatest losers, since their scheme turned against them.

Verse 70 of Surat al-Anbiya' describes the failure of the plot against Abraham. After losing the argument, his people planned to burn him to avenge their idols, and God turned their scheme against them, so they became the greatest losers. The commentators agree that the 'plot' was the burning with fire. Al-Sam'ani and al-Baghawi explain that the 'greatest losers' lost their effort and expense without achieving their aim, while al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi relate that God sent gnats upon Nimrod and his people, which devoured their flesh and drank their blood, and one gnat entered Nimrod's brain and destroyed him. Ibn Kathir, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi hold that their loss exceeded that of every other loser, since their attempt became a decisive proof that Abraham was upon the truth and they upon falsehood. Al-Tabari reports that the instigator may have been a Kurdish man from the Persian tribes, according to Mujahid and Ibn Umar, while others said it was Nimrod, and the exegetes did not settle the question. Al-Zamakhshari explains the choice of fire as the most dreadful punishment. On how the fire became cool, al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi say God removed its burning nature, others say God repelled its harm from Abraham, and others say a barrier stood between them. All agree that only his bonds were burned.

In this verse God saves Abraham and Lot, bringing them from the land of Iraq to the land He blessed for all the worlds. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and al-Baghawi agree that this is the land of Syria (al-Sham). Ibn Kathir cites a report attributed to Ubayy ibn Ka'b that every sweet water springs from the rock in Jerusalem, but several commentators treat this report as weak or unusual, and Ibn 'Atiyya considers it weak.

The commentators explain its blessing in several ways. According to al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Baydawi, it lies in the many prophets sent there, whose teachings spread through the world, and in its fertility, abundant water, trees and fruit. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi regard the blessing as both spiritual and material. Al-Shinqiti and Ibn 'Ashur note that it resembles the blessing given to the al-Aqsa mosque in Surat al-Isra.

They differ, however, on which land is meant. Ibn 'Abbas, as transmitted by al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir, identifies it as Mecca, citing the verse about the blessed House at Bakka. Al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi also mention Egypt, while al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Shawkani favour Syria, which they describe as the majority view.

Al-Tabari adds that no scholar disputes that Abraham's migration was to Syria, although he had visited Mecca and built the House there. As for Lot, commentators describe him as the son of Abraham's brother or as his nephew, and the accounts of the journey through Harran, Egypt and then Syria are traditions transmitted by Ibn Ishaq and al-Sudi.

This part of the verse says that God granted Ibrahim Ishaq and then Ya'qub, and made all three righteous, meaning obedient servants who fulfil their duties to God and to people. The commentators differ on the meaning of "nafila". Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Ibn Zayd and Ibn Kathir, followed by others, take it as an addition: it refers to Ya'qub alone, since Ibrahim asked for a child and received Ishaq, and Ya'qub was added without request as a grandson. Mujahid and 'Ata' understand it as a gift, applying to both sons. Al-Tabari notes that no proof settles between these readings. Al-Razi, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi prefer the sense of a gift or addition, while al-Zamakhshari holds that Ishaq was granted in answer to prayer and Ya'qub was given in surplus. On "salihin", most read it as obedience and uprightness, and al-Razi argues it cannot mean prophethood, since the revelation mentioned next would then repeat it. The commentators then report that God made them leaders who guide people by His command, revealed to them the doing of good, establishing prayer and paying zakat, and that they worshipped Him alone. Ibn 'Ashur and Ibn Sa'di stress this last point, and Ibn Kathir notes that these men practised what they taught.

This verse states that God made Abraham, Isaac and Jacob imams who guide people by His command, revealed to them to do good deeds, establish prayer and give zakat, and that they were worshippers devoted to Him alone. The commentators agree that the pronoun refers to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and that guidance means calling people to God's religion, while the divine command means revelation and permission. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi explain that 'good deeds' means acting on the revealed laws, and that the separate mention of prayer and zakat after them is the specific mentioned after the general, to honour them. Al-Zamakhshari draws the lesson that whoever is fit to be a model in God's religion is bound to guide, beginning with guiding himself, while Ibn 'Ashur sees these practices as the foundation of the original monotheism (hanifiyya) for which Abraham was sent. On the meaning of imam, al-Razi, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi understand guidance through calling and teaching, Abu Muslim takes it to mean prophethood, and al-Zamakhshari treats it as exemplary leadership in religion. On 'righteous', al-Dahhak takes them to be prophets sent, while others take them to be servants obeying God and avoiding His prohibitions, a view al-Razi prefers. Al-Razi and al-Jubba'i also debate the creation of human acts: the Sunni side finds an argument here, and the Mu'tazili side replies by interpreting righteousness as divine success and grace.

This verse says God gave Lot wisdom and knowledge, which the commentators explain as sound judgment or the authority to settle disputes, with some saying prophethood, and knowledge as understanding of religion. God saved him from the town, Sodom according to most commentators, whose people practised vile deeds. Most explain these as sodomy, and al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi also mention breaking wind in their gatherings and flicking pebbles, while al-Qurtubi and al-Tha'alibi cite a tradition that the town had seven settlements, six of which were overturned. All agree that these people were wicked and had turned away from God's obedience. They differ on the phrase "We admitted him into Our mercy". Muqatil, cited by al-Razi, takes it as prophethood, Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak take it as reward, and al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Qurtubi take it as Paradise or as deliverance. Ibn Kathir reports that Lot believed in Abraham and migrated with him to the land that God blessed, which most identify as Syria, though some name Mecca or Jerusalem. Ibn Sa'di adds that Lot called his people to worship God before being rejected and then saved by night, while al-Jaza'iri stresses that the wicked deeds were a cause of destruction.

The commentators explain that God mentions Lot after Abraham and says that He admitted him into His mercy, meaning among those He saved from the punishment that struck his people, because he was one of the righteous who obeyed God's command. They differ on what "mercy" means here. Ibn Zayd takes it to be Islam, Muqatil takes it to be prophethood, and Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak take it to be reward. Ibn Atiyya, al-Baydawi, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Nasafi understand it as the people of God's mercy or Paradise, and al-Alusi notes that Paradise is called mercy because it is its fruit. Most agree that his admission followed from his righteousness. The context also presents his rescue from the town that practised abominations as a blessing, and most identify these abominations as sodomy, while some add public flatulence and the throwing of pebbles. Ibn Ashur and al-Biqa'i place the verse within a series of favours granted to the prophets. Al-Razi understands mercy as prophethood given to one fit for it, and al-Sha'rawi sees it as the prophetic mission, which he judges fulfilled most completely in the mission of Muhammad, peace be upon him.

The commentators explain that this verse recalls Noah, who called upon his Lord against his people who rejected him, before the time of Abraham and Lot. God answered him, saved him and the believers of his household from the great distress, supported him against his people, and drowned them all. Most exegetes, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi, take "the great distress" to mean the flood and drowning, along with the rejection and harm he suffered. Ibn Abbas, as reported by al-Razi, combines both meanings, and al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir note that karb signifies an intense grief.

As for the call, most identify it with the prayers mentioned in Surat al-Qamar and Surat Nuh, such as "I am overpowered, so help me" and "Lord, leave not a single disbeliever on earth". Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di add that he preached for a thousand years less fifty.

The phrase "nassarnahu min al-qawm" has been discussed. Abu 'Ubayda, followed by al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan, reads min as meaning "against", while al-Zamakhshari links the verb to the sense of obtaining victory and avenging oneself. Ibn Atiyya and al-Biqa'i read it as protection from harm, a wording Ibn 'Ashur finds stronger than "against". Several authors, including Ibn Atiyya and al-Suyuti, finally note that the story serves as an example for the Prophet and a warning to the Quraysh.

The verse says that God gave Noah victory over the people who denied His signs, and because they were a people of evil conduct, He drowned them all. The commentators agree on the core meaning: the destruction of the entire people, caused by their rejection of the truth together with their persistence in wrongdoing, as al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud explain. Al-Qurtubi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi connect the verse to Noah's earlier prayer against his people, which God answered. The main disagreement concerns the meaning of the word for victory and its particle. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi understand that God protected Noah from them so that they could not harm him. Al-Mawardi offers two readings: either God granted him victory over them by answering his prayer, or He saved him alone from their fate. Abu 'Ubayda and al-Qurtubi take 'min' to mean 'against', and al-Razi mentions a reading attributed to Ubayy ibn Ka'b that uses 'against'. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Alusi observe that the verb implies both help and retribution, and Ibn 'Atiyya adds that since Noah's victory was chiefly his rescue, the particle 'min' fits better. On the word 'all', al-Nasafi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur state that none escaped, young or old, and Ibn 'Ashur specifies that Noah's own son drowned too. He also sees in the story a warning to the Quraysh who rejected the Prophet.

This verse recounts how the prophets Dawud and Sulayman, peace be upon them, judged a dispute over a field that a flock had entered at night and destroyed, with God as witness to their rulings. Commentators differ on the field's nature: a sown crop according to Qatada and al-Zuhri, a vineyard with forming grape clusters according to Ibn Mas'ud and Shurayh. Most understand nafash as grazing by night without a shepherd. Dawud ruled that the flock should go to the owner of the field as compensation. Sulayman, then around eleven years old, proposed a fairer arrangement: the owner of the field would take the flock and benefit from its milk, wool and offspring, while the owner of the flock would restore the field, after which each would return the other's property. Dawud accepted his son's view. Ibn Mas'ud and al-Hasan hold that Dawud erred without being blamed and that Sulayman was right; others say the rulings came by revelation, or that both were correct according to their own reasoning. Many scholars draw from this the permissibility of independent reasoning even for prophets and the possibility of an honest error. The verse then mentions the favours granted to Dawud, whose recitation the mountains and birds echoed, and his skill in making coats of mail, and to Sulayman, for whom the wind moved swiftly to the blessed land, and whom jinn dived for and served in other works under God's protection.

This verse recounts the case of David and Solomon concerning a field that sheep had grazed and damaged at night. The commentators report that David ruled that the sheep be given to the owner of the field as compensation, while Solomon proposed a fairer arrangement: the sheep would go to the field's owner to benefit from their milk, offspring and wool, while the shepherd would restore the field until it was as it had been, after which each would get back his property. God confirmed Solomon's ruling by making him understand the matter, and praised both prophets for their judgment and knowledge. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report that both rulings were ijtihad and that Solomon was correct; others, cited by al-Mawardi and al-Razi, hold that both were given by revelation, the later one abrogating the earlier. Scholars also debate whether prophets may err: the majority accept that they may err but do not persist in error, while others reject this. In legal terms, Malik and al-Shafi'i hold the owner of livestock liable for night-time damage but not daytime damage, whereas Abu Hanifa exempts him, citing the hadith that the injury caused by an animal is unpaid. The verse then mentions the favours given to David: the mountains and birds glorified God along with him, and he was taught to make coats of mail to protect people. Commentators differ on whether this glorification was literal, with most taking it so, or figurative. The verse ends with God's declaration that He is the One who does such things.

The commentators explain that this verse describes a favour God granted to David, who was taught how to make the labus, the armour worn in battle, which most of them take as the main meaning here. Qatada reports that armour had earlier been made of plates, and that David was the first to link it into rings, giving it both lightness and protection. According to Ibn Kathir and others, the phrase 'to protect you from your violence' means to guard you from the war of your enemies or from the strikes of weapons. The readings differ on the verb: most read 'yuhsinakum' with the ya, the subject being the armour, David or God; Ibn 'Amir and Hafs read 'tuhsinakum' with the ta; and Abu Bakr reads 'nuhsinakum' with the nun. Al-Tabari considers these readings close in meaning. The question 'will you not then be grateful?' is understood by most as a command and a rebuke, urging thanks to God for this blessing. Some report that God softened the iron for David, while others hold that this teaching followed ordinary causes, and a few draw from the verse the value of a craft and of earning one's living by work.

This verse states that God subjected the wind to Solomon, peace be upon him. It blew forcefully and moved at his command toward the blessed land, which al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi identify as Syria, where he had his dwelling, so that the wind would carry him there after taking him wherever he wished. The commentators agree that this subjection was a favour and honour from God to His prophet, and that God's knowledge encompasses all things, so that events unfold according to His wisdom. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others report that the wind carried Salomon, his armies and his equipment on a wooden platform or carpet, taking a month for the outward journey and a month for the return, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Baydawi explain that it was gentle in itself yet swift like a storm, combining both qualities, and that it could be gentle at one time and violent at another according to his will. Abu Hayyan, al-Nasafi and Ibn 'Atiyya note different readings of the word wind in the nominative, accusative and plural, without any change to the core meaning. Sayyid Qutb considers the details of the carpet and the journey unestablished and keeps to the apparent meaning of the verse, whereas al-Shinqiti and al-Sha'rawi clarify that the wind went where Salomon willed and returned him to his home in Syria. The verse also mentions the subjection of the jinn, who dove for pearls and performed other labours, and whom God kept from disobeying, as al-Tabari, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir state.

This verse tells that God subjected to Solomon a group of devils who dived for him in the sea to bring up pearls and jewels, and who performed other works besides diving, which the commentators name as buildings, statues, prayer niches, large basins and cauldrons. Al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan agree that the words "and We were their guardians" mean that God protects them from straying from His command or from spoiling what they have made. Al-Zajjaj and Ibn 'Abbas, reported by al-Tabari, add that when a devil finished his work before night, Solomon gave him another task so that he would not destroy what he had built. Al-Farra' and others understand it as keeping them from fleeing or from disturbing anyone. Al-Razi holds that these devils were disbelievers, since a believer does not need to be guarded from corruption. Al-Jubba'i, cited by al-Razi and al-Alusi, argues that God made their bodies denser as a miracle for Solomon and returned them to their original form after his death, a view al-Razi rejects. The commentators agree that the verse presents a favour granted to Solomon, and the surrounding context affirms the prophethood of Muhammad by recalling God's gifts to His prophets.

The verse recalls the Prophet Ayyub, who called upon his Lord saying that harm had touched him and that God is the most merciful of the merciful. The commentators agree that this harm was a severe trial affecting his body, his wealth and his family, and that he bore it with exceptional patience, so that he became a byword for patience. His call is understood as a humble supplication and a request for relief, not a complaint against fate. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others note that the detailed narrative of the trial comes largely from traditions of the People of the Book, some of them weak. They report that Satan was permitted to strike his property and children and then his body, and that his wife remained with him. The duration of the trial varies: seven years according to Ibn Abbas, Ka'b and Yahya ibn Abi Kathir, three years according to Wahb, seven years and six months according to al-Hasan, while a report from Anas speaks of eighteen years. Opinions also differ on what prompted his call, some saying Satan made him forget to pray for a time and others that he spoke when a worm fell from his body. As to the restoration of his family, Ibn Mas'ud, Mujahid, al-Hasan and Qatada say God returned his family by their persons and added the like of them, whereas 'Ikrima holds that they were kept for him in the hereafter and that he received their equivalent in this world. The verse concludes that this was a mercy from God and a reminder for worshippers, so that they may endure trials as he did.

This verse recounts that Ayyub, after the affliction that had struck him, called upon his Lord; God answered him, removed the harm that was upon him, restored his family and gave him their like along with them, as a mercy from Him and a reminder for those who worship Him.
