The commentators agree that Ayyub bore his trial in his body, his wealth and his household, and that his supplication was an indirect request, since he described his own condition, which calls for compassion, and called his Lord the most merciful of the merciful. On the meaning of 'harm has touched me', views differ: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others take it as a trial of the body together with the loss of wealth and children; Ibn Abbas and Qatada take it as sickness; al-Bukhari, relaying Anas, takes it as a statement of his condition rather than a complaint; others hold it was an admission of weakness or a plea for mercy. On the length of the trial, the reports from Ibn Abbas, Qatada and al-Hasan vary, and Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi prefer the report from Anas that the Prophet spoke of eighteen years. As for 'his family and their like with them', Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and Qatada say that they were restored to him in the same persons, while Mujahid and Ikrima hold that they were kept for him in the Hereafter and that he received their equivalent in this world. All agree on the patience this account teaches to believers.

This verse names three servants of God, Ishmael son of Abraham, Idris and Dhu al-Kifl, and describes all of them as among the patient. The commentators agree that Ishmael is the son of Abraham and Idris is Enoch, and that the patience praised includes perseverance in obedience, restraint from sin and steadfastness under trials. The identity of Dhu al-Kifl is disputed. Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, Mujahid and Qatada hold that he was not a prophet but a righteous servant who took on the duty of another pious man, such as performing a hundred prayers each day, or who guaranteed to a prophet that he would judge justly, fast by day, pray by night and never grow angry, and kept his word. Al-Hasan and most scholars say he was a prophet, and al-Razi and Ibn Kathir find this more consistent with the context, while al-Tabari leaves the question open. A well-known narration tells of a devil disguised as a wronged old man who tried in vain to anger him during his midday rest. Scholars suggest Elijah, Joshua or Zechariah as candidates. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya explain the word kifl as a portion, a guarantee or a double reward. All agree that God admitted them into His mercy because they were among the righteous.

This verse says that God admitted Isma'il, Idris and Dhu al-Kifl into His mercy, which the commentators explain as prophethood or the blessings of the Hereafter, because they were among the truly righteous. The exegetes say that these three were patient in obedience, in turning away from sin and in trials. Isma'il is the son of Abraham and Idris is Enoch. The identity of Dhu al-Kifl is disputed. Most scholars, including Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi, consider him a prophet, while Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, Mujahid and Qatada hold that he was a righteous servant but not a prophet. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir relate his story: he guaranteed to a man that he would fast by day, pray by night and never become angry, and he kept his word despite Satan's schemes. Proposed names include Elijah, Joshua and Zechariah. Al-Razi notes that the kifl can mean a double reward. Al-Tabari and al-Baydawi read mercy as prophethood, al-Baghawi as Paradise, and al-Razi as any good deed according to others. Righteousness, as the commentators describe it, covers the heart, the tongue and the limbs.

God recalls His prophet Yunus, the man of the fish, in the verse: 'And Dhu al-Nun, when he went off in anger...' The meaning the commentators share is this: Yunus left his people in anger after his preaching had gone on long and their stubbornness had worn him down, and he supposed that God would not restrict him or call him to account for leaving without permission. The phrase 'we would not have power over him' has several readings: al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take it as 'would not constrict him', a view supported by Ibn 'Abbas; Qatada, Mujahid, al-Kalbi, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj read it as 'would not punish him'; Ibn Zayd reads the clause as a rhetorical question of reproach. Several scholars, al-Razi among them, reject the idea that it expresses doubt about God's power.

The nature of his anger is also debated. al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr say he was angry at his Lord, while Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak say he was angry at his people. Ibn Kathir explains that after his people repented and God lifted the punishment, Yunus was vexed at being called a liar. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi link the anger to weariness at their obstinacy, and al-Zamakhshari adds that he should have been patient and awaited God's permission.

In the darkness, al-Tabari, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir report that the three darknesses are those of the night, the sea and the belly of the fish, while Salim ibn Abi al-Ja'd speaks of one fish inside another. His confession, 'There is no god but You, glory be to You, I was among the wrongdoers', is read as an acknowledgement of fault and a turning back to God. Al-Mawardi and others see it as correction rather than punishment, since prophets are not punished. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report the Prophet saying that no Muslim who calls on these words in distress is left unanswered, and this is why God adds: thus do We deliver the believers.

This verse reports that God answered the prayer of Yunus and rescued him from distress, and that this is His way with believers who call upon Him in hardship. The commentators agree that Dhu al-Nun is Yunus son of Matta and that al-Nun is the fish that swallowed him. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir report that Yunus left his people in anger after the punishment had been lifted from them, was swallowed by the fish, and called out in the darkness with the words of tawhid, glorification and confession of wrongdoing, and was answered. On the phrase "and thought that We would not decide against him", Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Dahhak and al-Tabari read it as "we would not constrict him" or "we would not punish him", while al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd read it as a question or as a supposition of God's inability; al-Razi, Ibn Juzayy and Ibn Hazm reject attributing doubt about divine power to a prophet. Opinions also differ on "mughadiban": anger at his people, at the king, or at his Lord, the last being rejected or reinterpreted by al-Qurtubi and al-Razi. As for the reading "nujji" with one nun attributed to Ibn Amir and Asim, al-Zajjaj and Abu Hatim call it an error, while al-Farra and Abu Ubayd justify it by an implied verbal noun; the majority reads "nunji" with two nuns.

God recalls His prophet Zakariyya, who called upon his Lord saying: My Lord, do not leave me alone without an heir, and You are the best of inheritors. Most commentators explain that he asked for a son who would inherit from him, either in prophethood, knowledge and wisdom, or by carrying on the religious mission after him, and that his closing words were a submission of the matter to God if no heir came. God answered him by granting Yahya and making his wife fit for childbearing. Most exegetes, including Qatada, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ibn Abbas in one report, state that she had been barren and became fertile. Others, such as Ata, Muhammad ibn Ka'b and al-Suddi, say she had a bad temper or a sharp tongue and God made her of good character. Al-Tabari holds that the wording covers both meanings, a view al-Qurtubi also accepts. The verse then praises these prophets for hastening to good deeds and calling upon God out of hope in His mercy and fear of His punishment, with humility. Commentators differ on who the pronoun refers to: some say all the prophets mentioned in the surah, others Zakariyya, his wife and Yahya. On the meaning of raghaban wa rahaban, most take them as hope and fear, while Ibn Atiyya and al-Razi give other readings, including ones tied to the position of the hands. Khushu' is generally understood as humble submission to God, and these qualities are presented as the reason for the answered prayer.

This passage of Surat al-Anbiya' says that God answered Zakariya's prayer, in which he asked for an heir so that he would not be left alone, granting him Yahya and making his wife fit for childbearing. The commentators differ on what this "setting right" means. Most, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Shawkani, hold that she had been barren and God made her fertile, while Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata' and Muhammad ibn Ka'b take it to mean that her character was improved, since she had a sharp tongue. Al-Tabari considers that the wording allows both meanings and that no evidence favours one over the other. The phrase "they hastened to good deeds" refers, for most, to the prophets named in the surah, and for some to Zakariya, his wife and Yahya. Hastening suggests eager and constant pursuit of good, like a traveller rushing toward his goal. They called on God with longing and fear: hope for His reward and dread of His punishment. Some add that the gesture of prayer differs with the mood, and Ibn 'Ata' explained the two gestures as asking and turning away from harm. Khushu', according to al-Hasan and Qatada, is humility and submission to God's command; according to Mujahid it is a lasting fear in the heart; according to Ibn 'Abbas it is sincere belief. Ibn Kathir finds these definitions close to one another, and al-Razi describes it as a firm fear in the heart that restrains from sin.

This verse speaks of Mary, daughter of Imran, who guarded her chastity, of the breath that God breathed into her, and of her and her son being a sign for all the worlds. The commentators agree that guarding her chastity means abstaining from all unlawful intimacy, that the breathing was by God's command, and that the phrase 'Our spirit' is an expression of honour. They also agree that the single word 'sign' refers to the one miracle of a child born without a father. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn Atiyya take the chastity to concern Mary's own body, meaning she kept herself from everything forbidden. Al-Mawardi, al-Sam'ani and Ibn al-Jawzi mention that it may refer to the opening of her garment, which Gabriel breathed through before she recognised him. On the breath, al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Baydawi explain that it was a breath of life given to Jesus in her womb, while others hold that Gabriel breathed and the breath reached her body. Several commentators list the wonders associated with mother and son, such as conception without contact, Jesus speaking in the cradle, and provision coming to Mary. Ibn Sa'di and al-Sha'rawi stress Mary's spiritual rank, while Ibn 'Ashur reads the image of breathing as a sign of swift creation.

The commentators explain that the verse declares the community of the mentioned prophets to be one community upon one creed, namely monotheism and submission to God, and that God alone is their Lord, so worship must be directed to Him alone. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and others, following Ibn Abbas and Mujahid, understand the word umma here to mean religion, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya note that it may address the community of Muhammad ﷺ and refer to the religion of Islam. Al-Mawardi offers two further readings: that mankind is one created kind, or one generation, and so should follow one religion. Most agree that the phrase 'one community' is a circumstantial description, though al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan discuss alternative grammatical analyses, including apposition. As for 'and they divided their affair among themselves', al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain it as people splitting into sects and parties over religion, with Jews and Christians departing from the message, while Ibn Juzayy and al-Alusi see the pronoun as addressing the listeners directly. Al-Shinqiti recalls that the Qur'an elsewhere condemns each faction's pride in what it holds. All agree that whoever does righteous deeds while believing will not have his effort denied but recognized and recorded. The following verse, which speaks of the impossibility of return for certain destroyed towns, is read in several ways: some take it as a refusal of repentance, others as not returning to this world, and al-Zajjaj as the rejection of their deeds.

The commentators explain that this verse follows the mention of the prophets and affirms that the community of the messengers is one community, grounded in worshipping the one God, and that the Lord is one. Most take the word "community" here to mean religion or path, and Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi understand it as Islam, which abrogates all other paths. Al-Hasan, Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan also consider that the address may be to the contemporaries of the Prophet or to all humanity. As for "they divided their affair among themselves," most read it as a split in religion into sects and factions, as al-Kalbi, Ibn Zayd and al-Tabari report, which produced Judaism, Christianity and idolatry. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Baydawi note a shift from direct address to the third person, which serves to condemn the act before others. They understand that each group made its religion into pieces to share out, as a group divides a possession. Ibn Ashur holds that the reference is to the polytheists, each tribe having taken its own deity. "To Us all will return" means, for all of them, that every group will return to God, who will judge them.

The verse closes with a threat to the divided and a promise to the righteous. Whoever does good deeds while being a believer will not have his striving denied, and it is recorded with God. Al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi explain kufran as denial or rejection, while Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di understand it as the doer's effort not being wronged. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi note that "min" in "some of the good deeds" is partitive, since no one can perform every act of obedience.

The verse says that whoever does good deeds while being a believer will not have his effort denied: God rewards him, does not withhold his due, and records his deeds. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi understand kufran as denial and the withholding of reward, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi see it as a figure for depriving someone of the reward, just as gratitude (shukr) is used for granting it, and the general negation serves emphasis. Most commentators take the recording as preservation and inscription in the book of deeds, and al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi add that the guardian angels write by God's command. Several scholars link the verse to the preceding one about the division of the community, while Ibn 'Ashur sees the promise to believers as placed right after the warning to unbelievers, and the writing as a metonymy for preservation.

The commentators explain this verse as stating that a people destroyed by God cannot return, either to this world or to repentance. The most common view, reported by Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima, Qatada and Ibn Kathir, is that God has decreed that the people of every destroyed town will not return to the world before the Day of Judgment, with the word 'lā' understood as superfluous for emphasis; in this reading, not returning means not repenting. Al-Tabari prefers this view, while noting that 'ḥirm' means 'resolve' and that 'lā' is a true negation, so that return means repentance and faith. Al-Zamakhshari takes 'ḥarām' figuratively, as what is impossible, and explains return as abandoning disbelief. Al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud accept both return to repentance and return to life. Al-Mawardi gives two interpretations, linking the first to 'Ikrima and the second to al-Hasan. Al-Zajjaj, as cited by Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi, understands that the deeds of such people will not be accepted, since they do not repent. Some scholars read 'ḥarām' as meaning obligatory, citing a line of al-Khansa'. Ibn 'Ashur holds that 'lā' is a real negation affirming the resurrection, an idea attributed to Abu Muslim ibn Bahr. The commentators agree that the verse leads into the sign of Gog and Magog breaking forth before the Hour, and they differ on the precise meaning of return.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the breaking open of the barrier that held back Gog and Magog, after which they will pour out swiftly from every elevated place on earth, a sign that the Hour is near. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and al-Baghawi largely agree that the pronoun "they" refers to Gog and Magog, that "hadab" means a raised place or hill, and that "yansilun" means they hasten, like a wolf running. They describe these peoples as two tribes of mankind, of very great numbers. Al-Tabari judges this the soundest view. Mujahid and others understand the pronoun instead as referring to all of mankind who will emerge from their graves to be gathered on the Day of Judgement, a reading supported by the variant "min kull jadath". Scholars also differ on the grammar linking this to the preceding sentence: some attach "until" to the prohibition on the disbelievers returning, others to an implied verb, and others treat it as a simple introductory particle. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya offer different readings of the closing clause. All agree that the verse ends by portraying the state of the disbelievers when the true promise, the Day of Resurrection, draws near: their eyes stare in terror, and they acknowledge their heedlessness and their wrong-doing against themselves.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the approach of the true promise, that is the Day of Resurrection, after the barrier of Gog and Magog is opened and they rush out from every elevated ground. The eyes of the disbelievers then stare in terror, and they cry out in regret: woe to us, we were heedless of this, and we were wrongdoers against ourselves. The commentators agree that the true promise is the Day of Resurrection. Most take the answer to 'when' to be 'then their eyes are fixed', while al-Baydawi and al-Razi, citing Sibawayh, take 'hiya' to refer to the event itself. Al-Farra and al-Kisa'i consider the waw in 'waqtaraba' superfluous, whereas the Basrans, as al-Zajjaj reports, assume an omitted answer: they will say 'woe to us'. Regarding 'hadab', Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Kathir understand it as a raised part of the earth, while Ibn Mas'ud's reading 'jadath' is taken to mean graves. Most say the subject of 'yansilun' is Gog and Magog, while Mujahid says it is all of humanity being raised. As for 'wa haram 'ala qarya ahlaknaha annahum la yarji'un', Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada take it to mean they cannot return to the world, al-Hasan to mean they will not repent, and others read the particle 'la' as superfluous or the word as meaning 'obligatory'.

God addresses the idolaters of Mecca: what they worship besides God, the idols, will be fuel for Hell, and they themselves will enter it. The commentators agree that the address is to the disbelievers and their idols. They differ on the meaning of the word hasab. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and Ikrima take it to mean fuel or firewood, and Ibn Atiyya notes this is the sense in the dialect of Yemen. Al-Tabari, following the reading with sad, takes it to mean what is hurled into the fire, as pebbles are thrown, and al-Dahhak adopts this sense, while the reading with dad, ascribed to Ibn Abbas, means what kindles the fire. As for the purpose, they see the punishment as increasing the shame and grief of the idolaters, and the phrase 'had these been gods they would not have entered it' as proving their falsehood. Scholars differ on whether Jesus, Uzayr and the angels are included. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi allow that the devils who commanded the worship are meant. Al-Razi holds that the verse concerns those worshipped who accepted it, and most exegetes say the word ma does not apply to rational beings. Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi relate the story of Ibn al-Zib'ari's objection and its answer, which they take as the basis for this view.

This verse addresses the idolaters of Mecca and the idols they worship: they and their gods are fuel for Hell, and if those idols were truly gods they would not enter the Fire. Both worshippers and worshipped will remain there forever, and the damned will groan with a painful sigh. The commentators largely agree on this basic meaning. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take hasab to mean fuel, while Mujahid, Qatada and 'Ikrima say it means firewood, and al-Dahhak says they will be hurled into the Fire as pebbles are thrown. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi note that ma is normally used for non-rational beings, which raises the question of whether angels, Jesus and Ezra are included. Al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report the occasion of revelation involving Ibn al-Zib'ara, who objected that Jesus, Ezra and the angels were also worshipped; the next verse, about those for whom the good reward has preceded from God, answers him. On who these exceptions are, Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima, al-Hasan and Ibn Jurayj name Jesus, Ezra and the angels, while others extend the phrase to all those destined for bliss. Al-Tabari and al-Baydawi mention that the idols themselves might be punished. Ibn 'Ashur reads the passage as describing the Day of Resurrection rather than a direct warning. The commentators do not settle these differences, and each presents his own arguments.

This verse states that the inhabitants of the Fire will have a zafir, a groan and laboured breathing from the intensity of their torment, and that they will hear nothing there. The commentators differ on who the pronoun refers to. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi understand the address to be to the polytheists and what they worshipped, so that worshippers and worshipped alike are in the Fire; Ibn Kathir notes that the verse was revealed about idols, which cannot reason. On the deafness, several explain it as the violence of the flames or as a sign that the damned will be gathered deaf, while Ibn Mas'ud, cited by al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi, says they will be placed in coffins of fire nested within one another, so that no one hears or sees another. Al-Zamakhshari sees the pairing of worshippers with their idols as a way of increasing their grief, and al-Razi adds that their gods do not answer their cries. On the following verse, the commentators agree that those for whom the good reward was decreed are kept far from the Fire, but they differ on who they are. The majority name Jesus, Uzayr and the angels, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir also citing an opinion that includes Uthman, while others take it as a general statement about anyone destined for happiness. Al-Wahidi and al-Baghawi report an occasion of revelation tied to Ibn al-Zib'ara's dispute, which Ibn Kathir considers unreliable.

The commentators explain that the verse "Those for whom the good reward has already gone forth from Us will be kept far from it" follows the description of the idolaters and their deities in Hell. It states that those whom God has destined for happiness will be kept far from the Fire, will not hear its roar, will not be grieved by the greatest terror, and will be greeted by the angels. Most agree that al-husna means happiness, divine success in obedience, or the glad tidings of Paradise. The verse was revealed in response to Ibn al-Za'bara, who objected that Jesus, Ezra and the angels were also worshipped; the Qur'an answers that one who is worshipped against his will is not like the idols.

Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report, through Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd, that the verse refers to those worshipped while obeying God, such as Jesus, Ezra and the angels. Others, including al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn Atiyya, hold that its wording is general and covers every believer who has been granted felicity. A report from Ali, which several authors cite, names Uthman among them; it is recorded without being presented as the sole meaning.

The commentators differ on the "greatest terror": al-Tabari and Ibn Abbas take it as the second blast of the trumpet, al-Hasan as the moment when a person is ordered to the Fire, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak and Ibn Jurayj as the closing of Hell over its people or the slaughter of Death. On the phrase about not hearing its faintest sound, some place it before entry into Paradise, others after the blessed have settled there, and others see it as an emphasis on their distance.

This verse describes those for whom the best reward has already been decreed by God: they are kept far from the Fire, so that they do not even hear its faintest sound, and they remain forever in what their souls desire. The commentators explain al-Husna as happiness, Paradise, or divine success in obedience, and al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report these meanings, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi list them together. The word hasis is taken by al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi to mean the sound or movement of the flame, and by Ibn Kathir as the burning of bodies, while al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir also cite a report from Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi about serpents on the Bridge that cry out at those they bite.

The occasion of revelation is widely reported. Ibn al-Zib'ara objected that angels, Jesus and Uzayr were worshipped, and commentators such as Mujahid, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi say that these figures are meant, while al-Razi, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan discuss whether the wording is general or specific. Ibn 'Ashur holds that it applies to every believer who dies in faith and righteous deeds.

As to the great terror that will not grieve them, al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, al-Razi and al-Baydawi mainly favour the final trumpet blast, al-Hasan the moment when a servant is sent to the Fire, and Ibn Jurayj and Sa'id ibn Jubayr the closing of the Fire over its people, Ibn Jurayj also mentioning the slaughter of death. Finally, the angels greet them, saying: This is your day, which you were promised. Al-Tabari and Ibn Zayd place this welcome before entry into Paradise, while al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi mention it at the gates of Paradise.

The commentators explain that the verse gives good news to believers for whom the best reward has already been decreed by God: they will be kept far from the Fire, will not hear its faintest sound, and will remain forever in the pleasures their souls desire. As for "the greatest terror will not grieve them", opinions differ. Al-Tabari, relying on Ibn Abbas and others, holds that it is the final blast of the Trumpet, reasoning that whoever is spared that terror is all the more secure from what follows. Al-Hasan al-Basri takes it to be the moment when the servant is ordered toward the Fire, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak take it to be the moment when the Fire closes over its people, and Ibn Jurayj takes it to be the slaughtering of Death. Al-Razi and Ibn Kathir report these same views, and al-Razi adds that it may refer to all the terrors of the Day of Resurrection.

They also differ over the meaning of "the best reward": Ibn Abbas, Ibn Zayd and Ikrima take it to be Paradise or felicity, Mujahid identifies those meant as Jesus, Uzayr and the angels who were worshipped without their consent, and others take it as a general rule for anyone granted felicity by God. The commentators also mention the occasion of revelation connected with Ibn al-Zib'ara's objection, though Ibn Kathir considers that report mistaken.

Regarding the angels' welcome, most explain it as congratulation and good tidings, given as the people rise from their graves or at the gates of Paradise. Ibn Zayd says it takes place before they enter Paradise.

This verse describes the Day of Judgment, when the heavens will be folded up as a scroll is folded over what is written on it, and God will recreate creation as He first created it, a promise He will certainly fulfil. The commentators largely agree that "sijjil" means the written sheet or scroll, as Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada held, and al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir adopt this reading. Most take the preposition "li" to mean "over", that is, as a scroll is folded over its writing. Others report that the sijjil is an angel who folds up the books of the children of Adam, a view attributed to Ibn Umar, al-Suddi and Ali, while Ibn Kathir and Ibn Atiyya consider the reports that it was a scribe of the Prophet weak. On the nature of the recreation, opinions differ: many, including Mujahid and al-Tabari, understand a resurrection barefoot, naked and uncircumcised, based on a hadith transmitted through Ibn Abbas, whereas Ibn Abbas in another report and al-Zamakhshari understand the annihilation and renewal of all things, and al-Zajjaj sees it as the equality of God's power over beginning and return. As for the supreme terror that will not grieve the blessed, commentators such as Ibn Jurayj, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi mention several views: the final blast of the trumpet, the closing of the Fire over its people, the slaughter of Death, or the moment the damned are driven to the Fire. All agree that believers will be secure and welcomed by the angels.

The verse states that God decreed, in the revealed scriptures after having recorded it in the Remembrance, the preserved Tablet or the Mother of the Book, that the earth will be inherited by His righteous servants. The commentators largely agree on the general sense. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take the Zabur to mean all the revealed Books and the Remembrance to mean the heavenly Mother of the Book, while al-Sha'bi understands the Zabur as the Psalms of David and the Remembrance as the Torah. Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak hold that the Remembrance is the Torah and the Zabur the books that came after it. As for the earth, most, including Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ibn Kathir, take it to be the Garden, while Ibn Abbas, in another report, means the earthly world that the community of Muhammad will conquer; Ibn al-Qayyim considers this second reading the sounder, whereas al-Qurtubi prefers the Garden, since worldly land is also inherited by others. Some identify it with the holy land or the lands of unbelieving nations. Most identify the righteous servants with the community of Muhammad, though al-Razi, al-Baydawi and Ibn 'Ashur sometimes widen the sense to all pious believers. The commentators also discuss the closing part of the passage: al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi explain that the Qur'an is a sufficient message for a worshipping people, and the mercy sent to all the worlds is widely read in the same spirit as a promise of success for the believers.

This verse states that what the Qur'an contains of reports, promises, threats and admonitions is sufficient and conveys its message to those who worship God, bringing them to what they seek: God's pleasure and reward. The commentators differ on what "this" refers to. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Tabari take it to mean the Qur'an itself; Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi refer it to the narratives, promises and threats of this surah, while al-Zamakhshari refers it to the weighty admonitions it contains. The word "balagh" means sufficiency, that by which one attains one's aim, and Ibn Kathir compares the Qur'an to the provision of a traveller toward Paradise.

Most exegetes understand "those who worship" as people who are obedient and humble before God, but they differ on who they are. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report from Ka'b al-Ahbar that they are the community of Muhammad, who perform the five daily prayers and fast in Ramadan; al-Qurtubi gives the same view from Abu Hurayra and Sufyan al-Thawri. Ibn 'Abbas describes them as people of knowledge or of action. Al-Razi holds it best to combine knowledge and practice, and Ibn al-Qayyim links worship with faith.

Regarding "We have sent you only as a mercy to the worlds," opinions differ. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Tabari, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir read it as a mercy for all: believers receive guidance and Paradise, while disbelievers are spared the total destruction that struck earlier nations. Ibn Zayd restricts it to believers, a view al-Baghawi also reports. Ibn 'Atiyya adds that the mercy may lie in the guidance itself, which each person accepts or rejects.

The commentators explain that God sent His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ as a mercy to creation, since he brought them what leads to their happiness in this world and the next if they follow him. Most, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi, hold that this mercy embraces both believers and disbelievers: believers receive guidance and Paradise, while unbelievers are spared the total destruction, sinking and transformation that struck the nations who rejected their prophets, their punishment being postponed. Ibn 'Abbas is reported to have said this, and al-Tabari chose this view. Ibn Zayd, by contrast, held that “the worlds” refers only to believers, a position that al-Nasafi and others record. Al-Razi and al-Alusi explain that the mercy appears in religion through guidance and the laying down of laws, and in this world through deliverance from humiliation and war. Al-Razi reports the Mu'tazilite objection that a mission cannot be mercy for those who disbelieve, and answers it by saying that deferring punishment is itself mercy. Ibn al-Qayyim argues that the mercy is for all, but that disbelievers rejected it, just as a cure benefits no one who refuses to take it. Several scholars cite the hadith “I am only a gift of mercy” and the report of the Prophet refusing to curse the polytheists. Al-Alusi extends the mercy to angels, jinn and humans, grounding this in the debate over the universality of the mission. The surrounding verses also state that the Qur'an is a sufficient message for those who worship God, and that the Prophet is commanded to deliver a clear warning to his opponents.

This verse tells the Prophet ﷺ to say to the polytheists that the revelation he receives is that their God is one God, and then to ask them whether they will submit. The question carries the force of a command to submit to God. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn 'Ashur all treat monotheism as the essential purpose of the prophetic mission. Al-Zamakhshari notes that the two uses of innama create a double restriction, the revelation being limited to the oneness of God and God's divinity being limited to His oneness, and he takes this to show that God's oneness can be known through revelation. Al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud follow him, while al-Alusi reports the objections of Abu Hayyan and the answers given to them.

The commentators agree that the phrase fa-in tawallaw means if they turn away. The meaning of adhantukum 'ala sawa' differs: al-Sudi reads it as on clear terms, Qatada as with a delay, al-Farra' as with justice, al-Kalbi as openly, and al-Hasan as meaning that those who reject the message are equal in facing jihad. Ibn Kathir explains that the Prophet is informing them of his enmity toward them just as they are hostile to him, and Ibn al-Jawzi gives two readings, a breaking of the covenant or an equal conveyance of the message.

On the words la'allahu fitna lakum, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Kathir say that the postponement of punishment is a test for them, while Ibn al-Jawzi notes the meaning of trial and of enjoyment until a set term. Al-Tha'alibi and al-Qurtubi record that the supplication rabbi uhkum bil-haqq was recited by the Prophet during battles, according to Qatada and Zayd ibn Aslam.

God instructs His Messenger to tell the polytheists that their God is one, and, if they turn away, to warn them openly and on equal terms, meaning without hiding from some what he tells others. He adds that he does not know whether the punishment promised them is near or far. The commentators agree that the address is to the Quraysh and that the word ádhantukum means a warning accompanied by a threat, announcing open hostility. They differ on the phrase 'on equal terms': al-Kalbi takes it as an open announcement, al-Zajjaj as equality in knowing what has been revealed, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi as an image drawn from the renunciation of a truce, and al-Hasan as equality in fighting between believers and unbelievers. As for 'what you are promised', Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari take it as the punishment or the appointed term, while al-Razi and Ibn al-Jawzi mention the victory of the Muslims or the Day of Resurrection. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi explain that the delay is a trial or a temporary enjoyment, whereas al-Zajjaj links the pronoun to the warning itself. The closing prayer, 'My Lord, judge with truth', is understood by Qatada as a request for judgment between the Prophet and his people, and by others as referring to the punishment that struck the Quraysh at Badr. The commentators conclude that the Prophet was given knowledge of the threat only, and that God alone knows when it will come.

This verse states that God knows what is said openly and what is concealed, and it serves as a warning to the polytheists that they will be judged for both. The commentators place it in the context of the preceding verses, in which the Prophet is told to inform the unbelievers that he does not know when the threatened punishment will fall, since that knowledge belongs to God alone. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the apparent meaning is that God knows the whole of the unseen and will requite both outward acts and inward intentions. They also report that the delay of punishment may be a trial for the unbelievers or a provision of enjoyment for a set time. Al-Mawardi lists several readings: the trial may be a destruction, a test, or a kindness, and the period of enjoyment may extend to the Day of Resurrection or to death, the latter being the view of al-Hasan and Qatada. Al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi specify that the open speech is the public attack on Islam, while the concealed matter is the resentment and hatred the unbelievers harbour against the Muslims. Ibn Ashur treats the sentence as a parenthetical clause that justifies the warning and explains why no one can know the timing of the punishment. The commentators agree on the substance of God's comprehensive knowledge and differ mainly over the precise identity of what is disclosed and what is hidden. The verse contains no legal ruling, and the exegetes read it chiefly as a warning and as consolation for the Prophet.

The commentators explain that this verse belongs to a passage in which the Prophet ﷺ is told to declare to the Quraysh that he does not know when the promised punishment will come, while God knows what they say openly and what they conceal. He adds that he does not know whether the delay of the punishment is a trial for them, and that it is a passing enjoyment until an appointed term. Most exegetes, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Baydawi, agree that the pronoun in 'la'allahu' refers to the delay or postponement of the punishment, and that fitna means a test or a lure that lets their disobedience grow. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir follow this reading, while Ibn al-Jawzi also records the view that the pronoun points to the warning the Prophet had just given. Al-Mawardi lists several meanings: fitna may be ruin, an ordeal or a kindness, and 'hin' may mean the Day of Resurrection, death, or God's decree concerning them. Al-Zamakhshari sees the delay either as a test to observe their conduct or as a respite that becomes evidence against them. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi also record the reading of Ibn Amir, who vocalises 'adri' with a fatha, which Ibn Mujahid rejected. A report cited by al-Qurtubi links the occasion of revelation to a dream of the Prophet about the Banu Umayya. Ibn 'Ashur explains fitna as a disruption of conditions that leads to harm, and mata' as a brief benefit. These commentaries draw no legal ruling from the verse.

God instructs His Prophet to pray: "My Lord, judge with truth," that is, decide between him and his people who denied him, either by bringing punishment upon them or by granting him victory. The commentators explain that the truth here means the punishment or the victory. Qatada reports that earlier prophets used to say: "Our Lord, judge between us and our people with truth." Al-Zamakhshari and others see it as a request to hasten the punishment, which came at Badr. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, also citing Qatada, report that the Prophet recited this verse when he faced the enemy in battle. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi suggest the meaning is "judge by Your true judgment," the noun having been omitted. Ibn 'Abbas, as cited by al-Tabari, notes that God only judges with truth, so the prayer is a plea concerning this world. All agree on the second part: "Our Lord is the Most Merciful, the One whose help is sought against what you describe," that is, against your lies, such as calling the Prophet a sorcerer or a poet, or claiming God has a son. Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi note that these accusations were tied to the pagans' hope of dominance and their belief that the threat would not come to pass. On reading, Hafs recites "qala" in the past tense, most readers recite "qul" in the imperative, Abu Ja'far recites "rabbu" in the nominative, and Ibn 'Amir reads "yasifun" in the third person. The commentators see the verse as closing the sura with the Prophet's trust in God against his opponents.
